title: Book 02 — Chapter 2, Session 2: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 2: Imam al-Hasan’s Pacifism (Session 2)
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Questions were checked against the original Session 2 chapter. The three elements of Imam al-Husayn’s uprising are compared separately with Imam al-Hasan’s circumstances; treaty clauses are stated from the source and their protective purposes are explained.

revision_policy: Keep Session 2 focused on the comparative historical circumstances and treaty clauses.
Distinguish the caliph in office from a protestor opposing an established government.
Explain the three elements of Imam al-Husayn’s uprising and why they differed in Imam al-Hasan’s time.
Treat the peace treaty as temporary and conditional, not as an unconditional endorsement of Mu‘awiyah.

questions.prompt: What central comparison does Mutahhari make between the political positions of Imam al-Hasan and Imam al-Husayn at the time of their decisions?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Imam al-Hasan was the caliph and rightful leader of the Muslims, while Mu‘awiyah was still formally a governor who had rebelled against him. Imam al-Husayn, by contrast, lived under a government that had already taken power and was a protestor against its corruption. If Imam al-Hasan had been killed while holding the caliphate, it would have meant the assassination of the caliph in office and a serious blow to the institution of caliphate. Imam al-Husayn’s martyrdom was the death of a protestor against an established oppressive government. Mutahhari argues that these different positions must be considered before comparing their decisions.
questions.source_locator: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn faced different political roles

questions.prompt: What was Mu‘awiyah’s formal political position when Imam al-Hasan became caliph, and what accusations had Mu‘awiyah used against Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Mu‘awiyah had not yet openly claimed to be caliph or Commander of the Faithful. He presented himself as a governor and rebel who refused to obey Imam ‘Ali, accusing ‘Ali of sheltering the killers of ‘Uthman and implying that ‘Ali was involved in the assassination. Thus, Mu‘awiyah framed his rebellion as opposition to an allegedly illegitimate government rather than as an open claim to the caliphate. Imam al-Hasan inherited the position of caliph after ‘Ali’s martyrdom and faced a rebellion from Mu‘awiyah.
questions.source_locator: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn faced different political roles

questions.prompt: Why would Imam al-Hasan’s death in battle have had a different political meaning from Imam al-Husayn’s martyrdom?
questions.answer: Imam al-Hasan was the caliph in office. If he had been killed while resisting Mu‘awiyah, the event would have been the killing of the rightful leader of the Muslim community and the defeat of the caliphate itself. Mutahhari compares this with ‘Ali’s efforts to prevent ‘Uthman from being killed while he was still caliph, not because ‘Ali supported ‘Uthman personally but because the assassination of a caliph would disgrace the institution of leadership. Imam al-Husayn, by contrast, was resisting an already established oppressive government as a protestor. His death exposed the injustice of the ruling system and became an honourable act of protest.
questions.source_locator: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn faced different political roles

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari describe the military balance between Imam al-Hasan and Mu‘awiyah?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam al-Hasan’s forces were weaker and less reliable than Mu‘awiyah’s. Historians estimate that al-Hasan might have assembled thirty to forty thousand soldiers, while some accounts suggest as many as one hundred thousand; Mu‘awiyah’s army is described as approximately one hundred and fifty thousand. The Iraqi forces were also divided and vulnerable to bribery, rumours, and betrayal. Mutahhari compares this with the earlier Battle of Siffin, where even Imam ‘Ali’s stronger army fought for eighteen months and was nearly defeated before Mu‘awiyah used the Qur’an-on-spears stratagem. A new war under al-Hasan would likely have been prolonged and destructive without achieving its goal.
questions.source_locator: The military balance made a long war unlikely to succeed

questions.prompt: What internal problems weakened the Iraqi forces and made a sustained war against Mu‘awiyah unlikely to succeed?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies disunity, betrayal, the influence of the Kharijites, and the presence of people who lacked discipline and a deep understanding of Islam. Many of Imam al-Hasan’s companions were unreliable, and Mu‘awiyah maintained agents in Kufa who distributed money and spread false rumours to weaken morale. The Imam was so unsafe that he wore armour under his clothes even when going to prayer, and he was once shot while praying. These conditions meant that a large army could not be assumed to be loyal or effective. A prolonged war would likely have caused mass casualties while leaving the underlying political problem unresolved.
questions.source_locator: The military balance made a long war unlikely to succeed

questions.prompt: What was the first of the three elements that compelled Imam al-Husayn to resist, and was it present in Imam al-Hasan’s situation?
questions.answer: The first element was the demand by the ruling government that Imam al-Husayn pledge allegiance to it. Imam al-Husayn refused to recognize the government through an oath of allegiance. Mutahhari says that this element was absent in Imam al-Hasan’s case: Mu‘awiyah did not demand that al-Hasan or his followers swear allegiance to him. The peace treaty explicitly did not require such an oath. This difference is important because Imam al-Husayn faced a direct demand to legitimize the ruler, while Imam al-Hasan’s agreement involved stepping aside without recognizing Mu‘awiyah as the rightful caliph.
questions.source_locator: Al-Husayn faced a demand for allegiance that al-Hassan did not

questions.prompt: How did the readiness of Kufa differ between the times of Imam al-Hasan and Imam al-Husayn?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Kufa was divided, exhausted, and unreliable during Imam al-Hasan’s time. Its people had shown a lack of preparation, and the Imam could not rely on them to sustain a war. By the time of Imam al-Husayn, after years of Mu‘awiyah’s rule, people in Kufa had sent many letters inviting him to come and lead an uprising. Mutahhari notes that eighteen thousand letters were sent. Even though the people later failed to support Imam al-Husayn, the invitations created an ultimatum that he could not simply ignore. The political meaning of Kufa’s invitation was therefore different in the two situations.
questions.source_locator: Kufah’s readiness to fight differed between the two Imams’ situations

questions.prompt: What was the third element of Imam al-Husayn’s uprising, and how did it differ from the conditions during Imam al-Hasan’s peace?
questions.answer: The third element was the duty to enjoin good and forbid evil in the face of an openly oppressive government. Mutahhari says that by Imam al-Husayn’s time Mu‘awiyah’s corruption, injustice, misuse of public wealth, and other violations had become evident. The duty to oppose such a ruler had therefore become clear. During Imam al-Hasan’s time, Mu‘awiyah had not yet revealed his full nature as a ruler and had made promises to follow the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice. The treaty allowed time for his conduct to expose the reality of his rule, making the later uprising of Imam al-Husayn more clearly justified.
questions.source_locator: The evidence of injustice had developed further by al-Husayn’s time

questions.prompt: What did Mu‘awiyah offer before the peace treaty was written, and how did he invite Imam al-Hasan to specify the conditions?
questions.answer: Mut‘awiyah sent a signed blank sheet and declared that Imam al-Hasan could write whatever conditions he wanted and that he would accept them. He promised to follow the Book of Allah, the conduct of the Prophet, and the way of the earlier caliphs. He also stated that he would not ask Imam al-Hasan or his followers to pledge allegiance to him or call him Commander of the Faithful. Mut‘awiyah presented the agreement as a temporary transfer of administrative authority under conditions that would protect the Ahl al-Bayt and the Muslim community. Mutahhari emphasizes that the Imam used this opportunity to set out specific protections.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: What did the treaty provide about the succession after Mu‘awiyah?
questions.answer: One of the treaty’s central clauses stated that after Mu‘awiyah, the government would return to Imam al-Hasan; if anything happened to him, it would pass to Imam al-Husayn. Mutahhari explains that this made the agreement temporary. Imam al-Hasan did not hand over the caliphate to Mu‘awiyah permanently or give him the right to appoint a successor. Mu‘awiyah therefore had no authority under the treaty to designate Yazid or another person as the next ruler. This clause preserved the rightful succession of the Imams and limited the transfer to Mu‘awiyah’s own period in power.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: What did the treaty require Mu‘awiyah to do regarding Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: The treaty required Mu‘awiyah to stop cursing and insulting Imam ‘Ali in prayers and public statements and to mention him only in a good manner. Mutahhari explains that this clause directly challenged the propaganda used by the Umayyads, who had tried to portray ‘Ali as an enemy of Islam. By signing the treaty, Mu‘awiyah formally agreed to stop the practice. The clause also exposed a contradiction: if Mu‘awiyah truly believed ‘Ali had departed from Islam, he would not have agreed to speak of him only with goodness. Mutahhari notes that Mu‘awiyah later violated this condition and the cursing continued for many decades.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: What financial provisions did the treaty include for Imam al-Hasan and the followers of the Ahl al-Bayt?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Muslim treasury, which had a balance of five million dirhams, was excluded from the transfer of government. Mu‘awiyah agreed to send Imam al-Hasan two million dirhams each year so that he could meet the needs of the Shi‘ah and his relatives without depending on the new administration. The treaty also included provisions for gifts and support for the Bani Hashim and for the families of those martyred alongside Imam ‘Ali at Siffin and Jamal, funded from the revenues of Dar Abjard. These clauses were intended to provide financial security and protect the community from economic pressure.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: What protections did the treaty provide for the safety of Muslims and the companions of Imam ‘Ali?
questions.answer: The treaty required that people throughout the Muslim lands—including Syria, Iraq, Yemen, and Hijaz—be safe and not be punished for earlier conflicts. It specifically prohibited grudges or reprisals against the people of Iraq and required that the companions of Imam ‘Ali be protected in their lives, property, families, and children. Their possessions were not to be confiscated, and they were not to be stalked, intimidated, or harmed. The agreement also prohibited overt or covert attempts to kill Imam al-Hasan, Imam al-Husayn, or anyone from the Prophet’s Household. These conditions aimed to prevent revenge and protect the community from political persecution.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say Imam al-Hasan’s peace agreement was temporary rather than an indefinite surrender of the caliphate?
questions.answer: The treaty explicitly stated that after Mu‘awiyah’s rule, authority would return to Imam al-Hasan and then to Imam al-Husayn if al-Hasan were no longer alive. The agreement also required Mu‘awiyah to follow the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice, stop cursing Imam ‘Ali, protect the Ahl al-Bayt and their followers, and refrain from appointing a successor. Mutahhari therefore argues that Imam al-Hasan did not permanently surrender the caliphate or grant Mu‘awiyah an unlimited right to rule. He stepped aside for a defined period under specific conditions intended to protect the Muslims and preserve the rightful succession.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: How did Mu‘awiyah violate the peace treaty after gaining power?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that once Mu‘awiyah secured power, he abandoned the conditions he had accepted. He did not follow the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice as promised, continued the hostility and cursing directed at Imam ‘Ali, and failed to protect the companions of the Ahl al-Bayt. He also began preparing for Yazid’s succession after approximately seven or eight years, despite the clause that placed the caliphate after him in the hands of Imam al-Hasan and then Imam al-Husayn. Mutahhari cites Mu‘awiyah’s own statement in Kufa that he had fought for leadership rather than to make people pray or fast as evidence of his political motives.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari explain the relationship between Imam al-Hasan’s peace and Imam al-Husayn’s later uprising?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that Imam al-Hasan’s peace helped prepare the historical and moral grounds for Imam al-Husayn’s uprising. The treaty gave Mu‘awiyah an opportunity to demonstrate whether he would honour his promises. When he violated the agreement, his true nature and the oppressive character of his rule became clearer to the public. This made Imam al-Husayn’s later opposition more justified and more easily understood as a response to established corruption. Mutahhari says that Imam al-Hasan deliberately allowed time for the reality of Mu‘awiyah’s rule to become evident, rather than launching a war under conditions in which the community was divided and unprepared.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances

questions.prompt: Would Imam ‘Ali have made peace if he had faced the same circumstances as Imam al-Hasan? What qualification does Mutahhari make?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the question cannot be answered by simply comparing their historical decisions. If Imam ‘Ali had been in exactly the same circumstances as Imam al-Hasan—including the threat of being killed while holding the caliphate—he too would have made peace. However, Imam ‘Ali’s actual situation was different: he was being asked to accept Mu‘awiyah as his deputy or representative, whereas Imam al-Hasan stepped aside and did not recognize Mu‘awiyah as a legitimate deputy. The treaty did not make Mu‘awiyah the Imam’s representative. Mutahhari therefore distinguishes accepting an unjust ruler as one’s deputy from temporarily withdrawing while setting conditions to protect the community.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances

questions.prompt: Compare the three main elements that led Imam al-Husayn to rise against the Umayyad government with the circumstances faced by Imam al-Hasan.
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies three major elements in Imam al-Husayn’s uprising. First, the government demanded that he pledge allegiance, which would have meant recognizing its authority; Imam al-Hasan was not asked to swear allegiance to Mu‘awiyah, and the treaty explicitly excluded such a demand. Second, the people of Kufa invited Imam al-Husayn through thousands of letters, creating an ultimatum that he could not ignore; during Imam al-Hasan’s time, Kufa was divided, exhausted, and had already shown that it was not prepared to support a sustained war. Third, the oppressive and corrupt nature of Mu‘awiyah’s rule had become clear by Imam al-Husayn’s time, making the duty to enjoin good and forbid evil unmistakable. During Imam al-Hasan’s time, Mu‘awiyah had not yet revealed his full nature and had offered written conditions. Mutahhari concludes that the two Imams faced different circumstances and therefore had different responsibilities.
questions.source_locator: Al-Husayn faced a demand for allegiance that al-Hassan did not

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari consider a prolonged war between Imam al-Hasan and Mu‘awiyah unlikely to achieve its intended purpose?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that Imam al-Hasan’s military position was weak compared with Mu‘awiyah’s. Even if al-Hasan had assembled thirty to forty thousand soldiers, or perhaps as many as one hundred thousand, Mu‘awiyah’s army was estimated at around one hundred and fifty thousand. The Iraqi forces were also divided, infiltrated by Mu‘awiyah’s agents, and weakened by bribery, rumours, betrayal, and the influence of the Kharijites. Mutahhari recalls that Imam ‘Ali’s stronger army had fought Mu‘awiyah for eighteen months at Siffin and was nearly defeated before the Qur’an-on-spears stratagem. A new war would likely have lasted years and caused thousands of Muslim deaths without defeating Mu‘awiyah. Imam al-Hasan would probably have been defeated and killed while holding the caliphate. Peace therefore prevented a destructive war that had little prospect of achieving its objective.
questions.source_locator: The military balance made a long war unlikely to succeed

questions.prompt: Explain the political and religious purposes of the main clauses in Imam al-Hasan’s peace treaty with Mu‘awiyah.
questions.answer: The treaty’s clauses were designed to limit Mu‘awiyah’s authority and protect the Muslim community during a temporary transfer of administration. First, Mu‘awiyah had to govern according to the Qur’an, the Prophet’s conduct, and the path of the earlier caliphs. Second, after Mu‘awiyah, authority would return to Imam al-Hasan and then Imam al-Husayn, preventing Mu‘awiyah from appointing a successor such as Yazid. Third, Mu‘awiyah had to stop cursing Imam ‘Ali and speak of him only with goodness, thereby ending a state-sponsored campaign against the Imam. Fourth, financial provisions were made for Imam al-Hasan, the Bani Hashim, the Shi‘ah, and the families of martyrs. Fifth, the people and especially the companions of Imam ‘Ali were to be protected from reprisals, intimidation, confiscation, and assassination. These clauses show that the peace was not an unconditional surrender. It was a temporary arrangement with explicit limits and protections intended to preserve the community and expose whether Mu‘awiyah would honour his promises.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: How did Imam al-Hasan’s peace help reveal Mu‘awiyah’s true character and prepare the ground for Imam al-Husayn’s uprising?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that Imam al-Hasan’s peace allowed Mu‘awiyah to assume power under conditions that he had formally accepted. The treaty required him to follow the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice, refrain from cursing Imam ‘Ali, protect the Ahl al-Bayt and their followers, and return the caliphate to Imam al-Hasan or Imam al-Husayn after his own rule. Once Mu‘awiyah gained power, he violated these commitments, persecuted the Imam’s followers, continued hostility toward ‘Ali, and began preparing Yazid’s succession. His conduct exposed the gap between his promises and his real political aims. Mutahhari says this made the injustice of the Umayyad government clearer to the public and strengthened the moral justification for Imam al-Husayn’s later uprising. The peace therefore served a historical purpose beyond avoiding immediate bloodshed: it allowed the ruler’s true nature to become evident.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances

questions.prompt: Explain the distinction Mutahhari draws between Imam ‘Ali’s refusal to accept Mu‘awiyah as a deputy and Imam al-Hasan’s decision to step aside under a peace treaty.
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam ‘Ali refused to accept Mu‘awiyah as his deputy or representative even for one day. In that situation, Mu‘awiyah was claiming a role within ‘Ali’s own government, and ‘Ali could not authorize an unjust person to act on his behalf. Imam al-Hasan’s situation was different. He did not appoint Mu‘awiyah as his deputy or recognize him as a legitimate successor; he stepped aside from the caliphate under a treaty that imposed conditions on Mu‘awiyah’s administration and protected the community. The treaty did not contain a clause making Mu‘awiyah the representative of Imam al-Hasan or the Prophet. Mutahhari therefore argues that the two decisions are not contradictory. The difference lies between accepting an unjust ruler as one’s own agent and temporarily withdrawing while limiting the ruler’s conduct through an agreement.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances

questions.prompt: What did Imam al-Hasan’s treaty require regarding the succession, the cursing of Imam ‘Ali, and the safety of the Ahl al-Bayt?
questions.answer: The treaty required that after Mu‘awiyah’s rule, authority would return to Imam al-Hasan and, if he were no longer alive, to Imam al-Husayn. Mu‘awiyah was not entitled to appoint a successor of his own. The treaty also required him to stop cursing and insulting Imam ‘Ali in prayers and public statements and to mention him only with goodness. It further required that people across the Muslim lands be safe, that the companions of Imam ‘Ali not be harassed or deprived of their property, and that no one threaten or kill Imam al-Hasan, Imam al-Husayn, or any member of the Prophet’s Household, openly or secretly. These clauses were designed to prevent dynastic succession by Mu‘awiyah, end state-sponsored hostility toward ‘Ali, and protect the Ahl al-Bayt and their followers from persecution.
questions.source_locator: The treaty’s clauses aimed to limit harm and define the transfer of power

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say that Imam al-Husayn accepted and followed Imam al-Hasan’s peace treaty rather than opposing it?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam al-Husayn was a follower of Imam al-Hasan at the time and accepted his brother’s decision. He does not find evidence that Imam al-Husayn signed the treaty, because his signature was not required; the agreement was made by Imam al-Hasan as the caliph. When opponents of the treaty approached Imam al-Husayn and offered to pledge allegiance to him instead, he refused and said that he would follow whatever his brother decided. Mutahhari emphasizes that Imam al-Husayn did not express even the slightest opposition to the peace agreement. This shows that the brothers’ actions were not contradictory: Imam al-Husayn recognized the authority and judgment of Imam al-Hasan and accepted the decision appropriate to their circumstances.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances

questions.prompt: Summarize Mutahhari’s overall argument for why Imam al-Hasan’s peace and Imam al-Husayn’s uprising were both correct responses to their different circumstances.
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that the two Imams faced different political positions and therefore had different responsibilities. Imam al-Hasan was the caliph in office, Mu‘awiyah was a rebel, the Iraqi army was divided and militarily weaker, and the people of Kufa were not prepared to sustain a war. The death of Imam al-Hasan would have meant the assassination of the caliph and the destruction of the caliphate’s standing. Imam al-Husayn, by contrast, faced a demand for allegiance from an oppressive government, received invitations from Kufa, and lived at a time when Mu‘awiyah’s corruption and violations had become evident. Imam al-Hasan’s treaty was temporary and contained conditions designed to protect the community and expose Mu‘awiyah’s real nature. When Mu‘awiyah violated those conditions, the grounds for Imam al-Husayn’s uprising became clear. Mutahhari’s conclusion is that the brothers shared the same commitment to truth and justice; their different actions reflected the different circumstances in which they had to fulfil that commitment.
questions.source_locator: Mutahhari says the brothers’ decisions were consistent with the circumstances
